why: Two numbers: == is ===, proved. A number-or-string against a string, the operands swapped: the table is symmetric, the string converted with one uninterpreted ToNumber on both sides, proved member by member on the union. A boolean-or-number against a number, swapped: the boolean becomes 1 or 0, proved. `n == undefined` is true on null while `n === undefined` never is on a number-or-null: unproved, witnessed on a null input. TypeScript itself refuses == between types with no overlap (TS2367), so the table matters on unions; Number(s) on a string makes a unit opaque, so a candidate cannot spell the conversion out.
